title: Do Inquiring Minds Have Positive Attitudes? The Science Education of Preservice Elementary Teachers
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether inquiry-based science content courses can improve preservice elementary teachers’ attitudes toward science. The authors focus on four attitude dimensions: confidence, enjoyment, anxiety, and perceived relevance. The motivating problem is that many elementary teachers report low confidence and negative affect toward science, which may in turn reduce science instruction quality and shape students’ attitudes.

The intervention studied is the Hands on Science (HoS) undergraduate program at the University of Texas at Austin. HoS is a guided-inquiry sequence of science content courses required for preservice elementary education majors, spanning multiple semesters and covering physics, chemistry, geology, biology, astronomy, and earth science. Students engage in hands-on investigations, small-group work, prediction, data collection, explanation building, and whole-class discussion rather than lecture-based instruction. A comparison group of noneducation, nonscience majors took traditional lecture-style undergraduate science courses.

The sample includes 238 preservice elementary teachers in HoS and 263 comparison students. The study is situated in a single U.S. university context and uses pre/post surveys with multilevel models to compare change over time. Results show that HoS students increased in confidence, enjoyment, and perceived relevance, and decreased in anxiety, while the comparison group generally declined in favorable attitudes. The authors conclude that inquiry-based content courses may help prepare future elementary teachers to enter classrooms with more positive dispositions toward science, with possible downstream benefits for their own students.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quantitative quasi-experimental study with a comparison group, pre/post measures, and multilevel models controlling for background covariates. It is not an RCT and the comparison groups differ in important ways, so credibility is strong but not definitive.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports modest-to-moderate positive attitudinal shifts in a priority population of preservice elementary teachers, with large relative gains in anxiety reduction and meaningful gains in confidence and enjoyment. Because outcomes are attitudinal rather than direct achievement measures, the overall impact is best characterized as green rather than blue.

finding.finding_summary: This quasi-experimental study found that preservice elementary teachers in the Hands on Science (HoS) inquiry-based sequence improved on multiple attitudinal outcomes relative to peers in traditional lecture-based science courses. In adjusted multilevel models (n=501 observations; HoS n=238, comparison n=263), the HoS × time interaction was positive for confidence (b=.500***), enjoyment (b=.391***), and relevance (b=.200***), and negative for anxiety (b=-.553***), indicating improved affect and confidence toward science over time.
finding.measure: Science attitude scales measuring confidence, enjoyment, anxiety, and perceived relevance

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was an inquiry-based science content sequence centered on scientific questions, experimentation, data analysis, explanation building, and evidence-based discussion. Although the paper did not measure scientific reasoning directly with a performance test, it substantively argues that the HoS curriculum developed students' engagement in scientific inquiry practices and their understanding of science as a process of discovery.
finding.measure: Participation in inquiry-based science content instruction; attitudinal proxies related to science learning
